## ARGUMENT

### A shotgun pleading that fails to give Defendant adequate notice of the claims against it warrants dismissal.

Rule 8(a)(2) requires "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief," and Rule 10(b) requires that claims be stated "in numbered paragraphs, each limited as far as practicable to a single set of circumstances." Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2), 10(b). This Court has long enforced those rules by condemning "shotgun pleadings," which it has criticized for decades. *See Strategic Income Fund, L.L.C. v. Spear, Leeds & Kellogg Corp.*, 305 F.3d 1293, 1295 & n.9 (11th Cir. 2002); *Cramer v. Florida*, 117 F.3d 1258, 1263 (11th Cir. 1997); *Anderson v. Dist. Bd. of Trs. of Cent. Fla. Cmty. Coll.*, 77 F.3d 364, 366–67 (11th Cir. 1996).

**1. The governing standard.** In *Weiland v. Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office*, 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015), this Court identified four recurring types of shotgun pleadings:

- a complaint in which each count adopts the allegations of all preceding counts;
- a complaint replete with conclusory, vague, and immaterial facts not obviously connected to any cause of action;
- a complaint that does not separate each cause of action into a different count; and
- a complaint that asserts multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendant is responsible for which acts or omissions.

*Id.* at 1321–23. "The unifying characteristic of all types of shotgun pleadings is that they fail to one degree or another, and in one way or another, to give the defendants adequate notice of the claims against them and the grounds upon which each claim rests." *Id.* at 1323. *Accord Vibe Micro, Inc. v. Shabanets*, 878 F.3d 1291, 1294–95 (11th Cir. 2018) (reaffirming the *Weiland* taxonomy); *Barmapov v. Amuial*, 986 F.3d 1321, 1324–25 (11th Cir. 2021) (same).

**2. Dismissal is the appropriate remedy.** A defendant cannot frame a responsive pleading, assert defenses, or conduct focused discovery when the complaint obscures which facts support which claim against which party. *See Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1320–23. This Court has therefore held that a district court has inherent authority to control its docket and to dismiss a complaint that violates Rule 8(a)(2) or Rule 10(b). *Barmapov*, 986 F.3d at 1324–25; *Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295. It has gone further and instructed that a district court confronting a shotgun pleading has a duty to require repleading, even if the defendant has not objected. *Jackson v. Bank of Am., N.A.*, 898 F.3d 1348, 1357–58 (11th Cir. 2018); *see also Magluta v. Samples*, 256 F.3d 1282, 1284 (11th Cir. 2001) (per curiam) (faulting a district court for tolerating a shotgun complaint and explaining the burden that such pleadings impose on the court and the parties). Shotgun pleadings consume scarce judicial resources, delay the resolution of meritorious claims, and force opposing parties and the court to guess at the claims actually asserted. *Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1356–58.

**3. Where repleading has been allowed and the defects persist, dismissal with prejudice is proper.** The usual course is to identify the deficiencies and give the plaintiff one chance to remedy them. *Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295. But when a plaintiff has had that opportunity and again files a pleading that does not give fair notice, the district court acts within its discretion in ending the case. *Barmapov*, 986 F.3d at 1325; *Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1358.

**4. Application.** Plaintiff's complaint exhibits the defects this Court has repeatedly condemned. [Conform to the record: (a) identify each count that incorporates all preceding counts by reference, with paragraph cites; (b) identify the counts that combine multiple claims or lump multiple defendants together without distinguishing the conduct attributed to each; and (c) identify the conclusory or immaterial allegations unconnected to any cause of action.] As a result, Defendant cannot determine from the face of the pleading which allegations support which claims or what conduct is attributed to it. That is precisely the lack of "adequate notice" that *Weiland* holds is fatal. 792 F.3d at 1323. Because [the district court identified these defects and afforded Plaintiff an opportunity to cure them / Plaintiff's pleading remains deficient], dismissal was warranted and should be affirmed.
